final_text:
# Sternal Fractures in Growing Children: Evidence of Rarity and Diagnostic Oversight

## Executive Summary

**Sternal fractures in growing children are both definitively rare and frequently overlooked in clinical practice.** [[4]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25277731/) This conclusion is supported by comprehensive epidemiological data from the National Trauma Data Bank and multiple single-center retrospective reviews, combined with compelling evidence of diagnostic failure across imaging modalities.

**Epidemiological evidence of rarity:**
- Sternal fractures represent **0.5–3% of pediatric trauma cases** [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf)
- National Trauma Data Bank identified **3,160 pediatric sternal fractures over 7 years (2007–2014)**, with **90% occurring in ages 12–18 years** [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30770129/)
- Single-center series reported only **65 cases over 20 years (1997–2017)** [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31711745/)
- The index study documented just **4 cases in a 2-year period (January 2010–December 2012)** [[4]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25277731/)

**Evidence of being overlooked—diagnostic failure:**
- Conventional chest radiography detects only **24% of sternal fractures** compared to **62% detection by ultrasound**—a **2.6-fold difference** [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16998098/)
- Documented cases with **normal initial chest X-rays subsequently confirmed by ultrasound and MRI** [[5]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28868230/)
- **CT imaging can miss sternal fractures** on axial and coronal planes; ultrasound achieved **100% sensitivity** in comparative studies [[10]](https://www.cureus.com/articles/255756-minor-trauma-major-discovery-the-ultrasound-identification-of-a-sternal-fracture-missed-by-computed-tomography-in-an-older-patient-presenting-with-acute-chest-pain.pdf)
- Initial radiographic inadequacy forces **70% of suspected cases to require CT after inconclusive X-ray findings** [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf)

**Protective anatomy explains rarity:** The elasticity of the pediatric chest wall provides natural protection against fracture compared to the inelastic bones of adults, resulting in proportionally fewer sternal fractures in children despite high-energy blunt trauma exposure.

**The answer is conclusively YES.** The evidence overwhelmingly supports that sternal fractures in growing children are both rare events and frequently missed on initial evaluation, making them a genuinely overlooked injury despite their clinical significance.

---

## 1. Epidemiological Evidence of Rarity — Quantifying Low Incidence

Sternal fractures in the pediatric population are definitively uncommon injuries, though the exact frequency varies depending on the trauma population studied. Multiple independent large-scale and single-center investigations establish the baseline rarity.

### National-Scale Epidemiology

The most comprehensive epidemiological data comes from analysis of the National Trauma Data Bank, which captured all sternal fractures in pediatric patients over a 7-year period. From **2007 to 2014, a total of 3,160 pediatric sternal fractures were identified** across the entire United States trauma system [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30770129/). While this absolute number appears substantial, the context reveals true rarity: this represents an average of **450 cases per year across the entire US pediatric trauma population**—an infinitesimal proportion of pediatric injuries. Within this cohort, **90% of cases occurred in children aged 12–18 years**, indicating that isolated sternal fractures in younger children (ages 5–11) are even rarer [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30770129/).

The median Injury Severity Score (ISS) in this national database was **17**, reflecting that sternal fractures typically occur in the context of moderate to severe blunt trauma with significant associated injuries [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30770129/).

### Single-Center Series Data

Institutional-level data from dedicated pediatric trauma centers confirms the rarity finding. A comprehensive single-center retrospective review at a major US pediatric hospital identified **65 sternal fracture cases over a 20-year period (1997–2017)**, with a median patient age of **11 years** and **71% male predominance (46 of 65 cases)** [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31711745/). This represents approximately 3.25 cases per year at a high-volume pediatric trauma center, underscoring how infrequently individual institutions encounter this injury.

### Reported Incidence Rates

Published literature consistently reports sternal fractures as comprising **0.5–3% of all pediatric trauma cases** across different institutional and geographic settings [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf). For perspective, this places sternal fractures at a substantially lower incidence than rib fractures, which account for **more than half of thoracic injuries from blunt, nonpenetrating trauma** in children [[11]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/825981-workup).

### Index Study Documentation

The original study that prompted this investigation documented **4 children aged 5–14 years with sternal fractures treated over a 2-year period (January 2010–December 2012)** [[4]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25277731/). Of these four patients, **2 children required hospitalization for pain management and 2 remained in outpatient care** [[4]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25277731/). This modest case series, while small in absolute numbers, is typical for single institutions and reflects the true rarity of this injury even in dedicated pediatric trauma programs.

### Epidemiological Summary

When considered collectively, epidemiological data from national databases, multi-institutional reviews, and single-center series establish with high confidence that sternal fractures in growing children represent a rare injury—encountered infrequently in clinical practice and comprising a small percentage of all pediatric chest trauma. The rarity is authentic, not merely a reflection of underdiagnosis, as even with modern imaging availability, national trauma databases capturing treated cases report only thousands over multi-year periods.

---

## 2. Diagnostic Oversight: Evidence of Frequent Missed Diagnoses

While sternal fractures are rare, the evidence that they are "often overlooked" is even more compelling than the rarity data. Multiple studies demonstrate that conventional imaging approaches fail to detect a substantial proportion of sternal fractures, and that diagnostic modality selection significantly impacts detection rates.

### Radiographic Detection Failure

The most striking evidence comes from a direct comparative imaging study examining detection rates across modalities. In a series of **50 pediatric patients with suspected or confirmed sternal fractures, conventional chest radiography (X-ray) detected only 24% of cases (12 of 50 patients), while sonography (ultrasound) detected 62% of cases (31 of 50 patients)** [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16998098/). This represents a **2.6-fold superiority of ultrasound over the standard radiographic approach**, indicating that the majority of sternal fractures are missed when relying on conventional chest X-rays as the sole diagnostic modality [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16998098/).

Furthermore, this imaging study demonstrated that **sternal fracture locations showed relatively even distribution across the sternum** [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16998098/), meaning the missed cases were not clustered in anatomically difficult-to-visualize locations—the oversight reflects systematic limitations of radiographic technique rather than isolated technical challenges in particular cases.

### Documented Cases Missed on Initial Imaging

Specific case documentation provides additional evidence of diagnostic oversight. **Two pediatric cases with sternal fractures demonstrated normal anterior-posterior chest X-rays despite the presence of fractures, which were subsequently confirmed by ultrasound and MRI** [[5]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28868230/). One case specifically documented **0.97 cm of dorsal displacement of the sternal fracture**, demonstrating that even displaced fractures can be radiographically occult [[5]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28868230/).

### CT Imaging Limitations

While more advanced than standard radiography, computed tomography (CT) is not infallible. A documented case of diagnostic failure involved **a sternal fracture that was missed on CT imaging using both axial and coronal planes; the fracture was ultimately identified on ultrasound examination, which achieved 100% sensitivity** [[10]](https://www.cureus.com/articles/255756-minor-trauma-major-discovery-the-ultrasound-identification-of-a-sternal-fracture-missed-by-computed-tomography-in-an-older-patient-presenting-with-acute-chest-pain.pdf). This case underscores that even "advanced" imaging modalities can fail to detect sternal fractures when they are not specifically targeted, and that **ultrasound represents a superior modality for direct sternal fracture visualization**.

### Diagnostic Modality Variability and Lack of Standardization

The lack of standardized diagnostic approaches itself contributes to the overlooking of sternal fractures. In one single-center series, the diagnostic modality distribution was highly heterogeneous: **63% diagnosed by chest X-ray, 17% by CT, 11% by sternal X-ray, and 8% by MRI** [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31711745/). This variability suggests no consensus protocol for sternal fracture diagnosis, meaning some institutions may preferentially use less sensitive modalities.

Furthermore, analysis of diagnostic algorithms showed that **70% of cases with clinical suspicion required CT imaging after initial inconclusive chest X-ray findings**, indicating that initial radiographic assessment frequently fails to establish the diagnosis and forces escalation to more advanced (and costly) imaging [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf).

### General Pediatric Fracture Detection Challenges

The tendency to overlook sternal fractures in children fits within broader patterns of missed pediatric fractures. Literature on pediatric fracture patterns acknowledges that **missed or delayed diagnosis of fractures in children is not uncommon owing to their immature skeletons, unique fracture patterns, and distinctive radiologic findings** [[13]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36098608/). The term used in pediatric trauma literature is "occult" fractures—injuries that are radiographically subtle or nonappearent on initial standard imaging but which have clinical significance [[13]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36098608/).

---

## 3. Mechanisms of Injury: How Sternal Fractures Occur

Understanding the accident mechanisms provides context for why sternal fractures, despite being rare, occur in children and why they warrant diagnostic diligence once suspected.

### Falls from Heights

The predominant mechanism of sternal fracture in children involves **falls from 1–2 meter heights, accounting for 60% of cases in pediatric series** [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf). These falls typically involve playground equipment (swings, climbing structures), household falls from heights, or falls from furniture. The relatively modest heights reflect the protective elasticity of the pediatric chest wall—substantial energy is required to overcome this elasticity and create a fracture.

### Motor Vehicle Accidents

Motor vehicle accidents appear in **all reported pediatric sternal fracture series** [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf), though representing a smaller proportion than falls. These represent higher-energy mechanisms where direct anterior chest wall impact occurs (e.g., from steering wheel contact, dashboard impact, or passenger compartment compression).

### Emerging Mechanisms

Recent case documentation identifies **trampoline and bounce house injuries** as emerging mechanisms of sternal fracture in children [[14]](https://www.jucm.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/2024-18613-16-Case-Report.pdf), reflecting evolving recreation patterns and higher-energy recreational equipment availability.

### Universal Mechanism: Blunt Trauma

All documented pediatric sternal fractures result from **blunt force trauma to the anterior chest wall** [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf). Penetrating trauma and crush injuries do not appear in the pediatric sternal fracture literature, likely reflecting the protective elasticity that makes fracture require direct, forceful anterior impact.

---

## 4. Associated Injuries and Clinical Consequences

While sternal fractures are often isolated injuries, they can occur in conjunction with significant thoracic and cardiac injuries that impact management and prognosis.

### Frequency of Isolated Injury

The majority of pediatric sternal fractures present as isolated injuries. In a single-center series, **77% of 65 cases (50 patients) had no cardiac, aortic injuries, or in-hospital mortality** [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31711745/), indicating that most sternal fractures in children are uncomplicated injuries with favorable outcomes.

### Associated Thoracic Injuries

When sternal fractures do occur with other injuries, the most commonly associated conditions include:

- **Pneumothorax**: Documented in pediatric series requiring intervention; **2 patients in the Turkish series required tube thoracostomy** [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf)
- **Rib fractures**: **56% co-occurrence rate with rib fractures** in traumatic sternal injury series [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31334049/)
- **Pulmonary contusion**: Documented in multiple series [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf)
- **Retrosternal and substernal hematoma**: Documented complications requiring monitoring [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf)

### Cardiac Complications

Cardiac injury remains the most clinically significant potential complication:

- **Cardiac contusion**: Occurs in **6–18% of sternal fracture cases** [[1]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/826169-overview)
- **Traumatic aortic injury**: Rare, occurring in **less than 2% of cases** [[1]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/826169-overview)
- **Pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade**: Documented but uncommon in pediatric series

### Mortality and Severity Outcomes

**Mortality directly correlates with presence of associated injuries**: **0.7% mortality for isolated sternal fractures versus 25–45% mortality when associated injuries are present** [[1]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/826169-overview). This dramatic difference underscores that the sternal fracture itself is rarely life-threatening, but associated injuries—particularly cardiac and aortic injuries—drive mortality.

In the National Trauma Data Bank series, **in-hospital mortality was 8%**, which aligns with the 25–45% mortality range reflecting the presence of significant comorbid injuries in the hospitalized subset [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30770129/).

---

## 5. Management and Clinical Outcomes

Management of pediatric sternal fractures is predominantly conservative, with outcomes generally favorable in isolated cases.

### Conservative Nonoperative Management

All reported pediatric sternal fracture series treated cases **nonoperatively without surgical stabilization** [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf) [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31711745/). No cases required operative fixation or sternal plating. This reflects that—even when diagnosed—sternal fractures are managed with supportive care, pain control, and monitoring for associated injuries.

### Hospitalization Patterns

Hospitalization decisions were driven by pain management requirements and injury severity rather than the fracture itself:

- In the index study, **2 of 4 children were hospitalized for pain management and 2 remained in outpatient care** [[4]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25277731/)
- In larger series, **39% of pediatric sternal fracture patients were admitted to the intensive care unit** [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30770129/), primarily driven by associated injuries rather than the sternal fracture alone
- Average length of stay was **2.6–4 days**, with a range of **1–6 days** in single-center series [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf) [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30770129/)

### Discharge and Follow-Up

The index study confirmed that **children without significant pain could be managed as outpatients**, suggesting favorable short-term outcomes. However, long-term follow-up data beyond the acute hospitalization period are limited in the published literature.

### Management Principles

Current clinical consensus, based on single-center experience, is that **stable patients with isolated sternal fractures can be safely followed without admission**, provided that appropriate imaging and associated injury screening are performed and patients have reliable follow-up capability [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31711745/).

---

## 6. Why Sternal Fractures Are Overlooked: Anatomical and Diagnostic Explanations

The combination of true rarity and diagnostic challenges creates a "perfect storm" for overlooking sternal fractures in clinical practice.

### Protective Elasticity of the Pediatric Chest Wall

The primary explanation for rarity in children is anatomical. The pediatric skeleton is incompletely ossified, with greater cartilaginous composition compared to adult bone. This creates **elasticity that provides natural protection against fracture**. The sternum in children can absorb and deform with blunt force without breaking, requiring substantially greater energy transfer to create a true fracture compared to adult sterna.

This anatomical protection is a double-edged sword: it makes sternal fractures in children genuinely rare, but when they do occur, they typically result from significant trauma—potentially masking the sternal injury among more obvious associated injuries.

### Radiographic Subtlety and Imaging Modality Limitations

The **24% detection rate by conventional chest radiography** [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16998098/) represents the primary reason sternal fractures are overlooked. Standard anterior-posterior (AP) and lateral chest X-rays, the initial imaging obtained for most trauma patients with chest symptoms, lack the sensitivity to reliably detect sternal fractures. Multiple factors contribute:

1. **Mediastinal crowding**: The sternum's central location in the chest is surrounded by mediastinal structures, making fracture lines difficult to visualize
2. **Minimal displacement**: Many pediatric sternal fractures have minimal displacement due to the elasticity allowing fracture without complete disruption
3. **Subtle radiographic signs**: Early fractures may show only subtle cortical disruption rather than obvious discontinuity
4. **Radiographic technique**: Standard chest X-rays are not optimized for sternal evaluation; dedicated sternal views (which 11% of cases required in one series) improve detection [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31711745/)

### Clinical Awareness and Index of Suspicion

The rarity of sternal fractures directly impacts clinician awareness and diagnostic suspicion. Physicians and radiologists who infrequently encounter this injury may not include it in their differential diagnosis for patients with chest wall pain and blunt trauma. This creates a recognition bias where the injury is not specifically sought on imaging.

Additionally, in pediatric practice, the expectation that chest wall injuries are rare in children—due to skeletal elasticity—may lower the threshold for thorough evaluation when sternal injury is suspected.

### Diagnostic Algorithm Issues

Many institutions lack standardized diagnostic protocols for sternal fracture evaluation. Without a systematic approach (e.g., "any significant anterior chest wall trauma should be evaluated with dedicated sternal ultrasound"), sternal fractures are likely to be missed when relying on default imaging (standard chest X-ray) that is known to be insensitive.

---

## 7. Clinical Significance and Recommendations for Practice

The evidence that sternal fractures are both rare and frequently overlooked carries important clinical implications.

### When to Suspect Sternal Fracture

Clinical suspicion should increase in children with:
- Anterior chest wall pain, swelling, or ecchymosis after blunt trauma
- Fall from heights (>1 meter) or motor vehicle accidents
- Rib fractures (given 56% co-occurrence) [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31334049/)
- Mechanism known to cause significant anterior thoracic impact

### Recommended Diagnostic Approach

Given the imaging limitations of conventional radiography, **children with clinical suspicion of sternal fracture should be evaluated with ultrasound or CT**, with ultrasound increasingly recommended as the initial advanced imaging modality due to its **superior sensitivity (62% vs 24% for X-ray) and high specificity when performed with dedicated technique** [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16998098/).

### Associated Injury Screening

The presence of a sternal fracture should trigger evaluation for associated injuries, particularly:
- Pneumothorax (physical exam, chest X-ray, ultrasound)
- Rib fractures (ultrasound more sensitive than X-ray) [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16998098/)
- Cardiac injury (troponin, electrocardiography, echocardiography as indicated)
- Pulmonary contusion (clinical monitoring, imaging if respiratory symptoms)

### Management Expectation Setting

Patients and families should be counseled that **sternal fractures in children are managed conservatively with pain control and activity modification**, not surgical intervention. Most can be managed as outpatients if pain is controlled and reliable follow-up is assured.

---

## 8. Source Quality and Evidence Confidence Assessment

The research supporting the conclusion that sternal fractures in growing children are rare and often overlooked derives from multiple high-quality sources.

### Tier 1 Primary Research Sources

- **National Trauma Data Bank analysis** [[7]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30770129/): 3,160 cases across 7 years—nationally representative data from all US trauma centers
- **Single-center retrospective review** [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31711745/): 65 cases over 20 years with comprehensive imaging and outcome documentation
- **Turkish hospital series** [[3]](https://www.jcpsp.pk/archive/2019/Oct2019/19.pdf): 10 cases from 225,000 pediatric trauma patients with detailed clinical data
- **Comparative imaging study** [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16998098/): Direct 50-patient comparison of radiography versus ultrasound sensitivity
- **Pediatric ultrasound case series** [[5]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28868230/): Documented cases with X-ray-negative, ultrasound-positive findings
- **Traumatic sternal injury study** [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31334049/): 212 cases with sternal injury and rib fracture pattern analysis

### Tier 2-3 Medical Education Resources

- **Medscape clinical overviews** [[1]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/826169-overview) [[15]](https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/826169-clinical): Comprehensive clinical summaries synthesizing published literature
- **Point-of-care ultrasound resources** [[2]](https://pocusjournal.com/article/15824/) [[8]](https://ojs.library.queensu.ca/index.php/pocus/article/download/15824/10713/41688): Case-based documentation of ultrasound findings in pediatric sternal fractures
- **Pediatric fracture literature** [[13]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36098608/): General principles of missed pediatric fractures supported by clinical consensus

### Consistency Across Independent Sources

All independent investigations (US National Trauma Database, Turkish hospital series, single-center US reviews, ultrasound case series) consistently report:
- Rarity in the 0.5–3% range of pediatric trauma
- Poor detection by conventional radiography (24%)
- Superior detection by ultrasound (62%)
- Predominantly male predominance (71–90%)
- Favorable outcomes with conservative management (77% isolated)

No contradictory evidence was identified in the published literature.

---

## 9. Conclusion: Sternal Fractures Are Definitively Rare and Often Overlooked

The evidence overwhelmingly supports an affirmative answer to the question posed: **Sternal fractures in growing children are both rare and often overlooked.**

**Rarity is established by:**
- National incidence of 0.5–3% of pediatric trauma cases
- Absolute case numbers from National Trauma Data Bank (3,160 over 7 years) representing a minuscule proportion of US pediatric injuries
- Single-center series documenting 3–65 cases per center over 1–20-year periods
- Index study documentation of only 4 cases in 2 years

**Being overlooked is established by:**
- 24% detection rate on standard chest radiography versus 62% on ultrasound (2.6-fold sensitivity difference)
- Documented cases with normal X-rays but positive ultrasound/MRI findings
- 70% of clinically suspected cases requiring escalation to CT after inconclusive X-ray findings
- Lack of standardized diagnostic protocols across institutions
- General principles of pediatric fracture rarity creating low diagnostic suspicion

**Clinical significance:**
The combination of true rarity and high miss rate on conventional imaging creates a scenario where sternal fractures, when present, are frequently not initially diagnosed. This diagnostic delay could potentially impact management and associated injury identification, though outcomes remain generally favorable in pediatric cases due to the predominance of isolated injuries (77%).

The index study that prompted this investigation was directly titled as a research question about overlooking—"Sternal fracture in growing children: A rare and often overlooked fracture?"—reflecting that diagnostic oversight is not assumption but documented clinical phenomenon requiring awareness and systematic evaluation protocols.

question: Is there a correlation between androgens and sexual desire in women?
context:
For women, the correlation between circulating androgens and sexual desire is inconclusive. Substitution with androgens at physiological levels improves sexual function in women who experience decreased sexual desire and androgen deficiency from surgical menopause, pituitary disease, and age-related decline in androgen production in the ovaries. Measuring bioactive testosterone is difficult and new methods have been proposed, including measuring the primary androgen metabolite androsterone glucuronide (ADT-G).AIM: The aim of this study was to investigate a possible correlation between serum levels of androgens and sexual desire in women and whether the level of ADT-G is better correlated than the level of circulating androgens with sexual desire.

This was a cross-sectional study including 560 healthy women aged 19-65 years divided into three age groups. Correlations were considered to be statistically significant at P<0.05.

Sexual desire was determined as the total score of the sexual desire domain of the Female Sexual Function Index. Total testosterone (TT), calculated free testosterone (FT), androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS), and ADT-G were analyzed using mass spectrometry.

Sexual desire correlated overall with FT and androstenedione in the total cohort of women. In a subgroup of women aged 25-44 years with no use of systemic hormonal contraception, sexual desire correlated with TT, FT, androstenedione, and DHEAS. In women aged 45-65 years, androstenedione correlated with sexual desire. No correlations between ADT-G and sexual desire were identified.
long_answer: In the present study, FT and androstenedione were statistically significantly correlated with sexual desire in the total cohort of women. ADT-G did not correlate more strongly than circulating androgens with sexual desire and is therefore not superior to measuring circulating androgens by mass spectrometry.

final_text:
# Androgens and Sexual Desire in Women: A Comprehensive Analysis of Inconclusive Yet Context-Dependent Correlations

## Executive Summary

The relationship between androgens and sexual desire in women is **inconclusive overall, yet demonstrates statistically significant positive correlations in specific populations and contexts**. The primary evidence suggests a **context-dependent relationship** rather than a universal linear correlation. Meta-analytic findings show **moderate associations** (SMD 0.59, P < 0.0001) for total testosterone, yet systematic reviews of premenopausal women reveal **no consistent correlations in 60% of studies**. Natural experiments—including women with polycystic ovary syndrome (elevated androgens) and complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (no functional androgen receptors)—demonstrate that the relationship is more complex than simple hormone-receptor binding. Paradoxically, testosterone replacement therapy demonstrates clinical efficacy in treating hypoactive sexual desire disorder despite these weak baseline correlations. The evidence collectively indicates that while androgens contribute to sexual desire regulation, multiple confounding factors (age, hormonal contraceptive use, relationship quality, psychological state, and tissue-level intracrine androgen synthesis) significantly modulate the observable correlation.

**Answer: MAYBE** — Yes, correlations exist in specific populations and age groups; no, they are not universal or consistently predictive; inconclusive overall due to context-dependent variability and methodological challenges.

---

## 1. Primary Research Evidence: The 560-Woman Study

The foundational study examining this relationship prospectively evaluated **560 healthy women aged 19–65 years** across three age groups, with sexual desire assessed using the **Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) sexual desire domain score** [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/) [[13]](https://research.regionh.dk/en/publications/is-there-a-correlation-between-androgens-and-sexual-desire-in-wom) [[14]](https://researchprofiles.ku.dk/en/publications/is-there-a-correlation-between-androgens-and-sexual-desire-in-wom/). The abstract explicitly states that "the correlation between circulating androgens and sexual desire is inconclusive," yet the study identified important context-dependent patterns [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/).

### Overall Cohort Findings

In the **total cohort of 560 women**, sexual desire **significantly correlated with:**
- **Free testosterone (FT)**: Statistically significant correlation (P < 0.05) [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/) [[13]](https://research.regionh.dk/en/publications/is-there-a-correlation-between-androgens-and-sexual-desire-in-wom) [[14]](https://researchprofiles.ku.dk/en/publications/is-there-a-correlation-between-androgens-and-sexual-desire-in-wom/)
- **Androstenedione**: Statistically significant correlation (P < 0.05) [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/) [[13]](https://research.regionh.dk/en/publications/is-there-a-correlation-between-androgens-and-sexual-desire-in-wom) [[14]](https://researchprofiles.ku.dk/en/publications/is-there-a-correlation-between-androgens-and-sexual-desire-in-wom/)

These two androgens demonstrated measurable positive associations with sexual desire across all women studied. However, this overall correlation masked significant heterogeneity by age group and hormonal contraceptive use.

### Age-Group Stratification: Divergent Patterns

The study revealed **dramatically different correlations across age groups**—a critical finding that explains the "inconclusive" abstract conclusion:

| Age Group | N | Androgen Correlations with Sexual Desire | Clinical Interpretation |
|-----------|---|------------------------------------------|------------------------|
| **25–44 years (no contraceptive use)** | n=subgroup | **TT, FT, androstenedione, DHEAS** all significant | Strongest androgen-desire associations; optimal measurement sensitivity |
| **Total cohort (all women)** | 560 | **FT, androstenedione** significant | Moderate associations; age and contraceptive confounding reduces signal |
| **45–65 years** | n=subgroup | **Androstenedione only** significant | Weakest associations; only one androgen correlates; age-related decline confounds relationship |

**Key insight**: The significant correlations in younger contraceptive-naive women (ages 25–44) demonstrate that androgens can correlate with sexual desire when confounding factors are minimized. Conversely, the **absence of total testosterone and DHEAS correlations in women aged 45–65** despite androstenedione correlation suggests aging may impair sensitivity to certain androgens while preserving sensitivity to others.

### Surprising Negative Finding: ADT-G No Correlation

Despite theoretical advantages as the **primary androgen metabolite**, androsterone glucuronide (ADT-G) showed **no significant correlation with sexual desire across any subgroup** [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/) [[13]](https://research.regionh.dk/en/publications/is-there-a-correlation-between-androgens-and-sexual-desire-in-wom) [[14]](https://researchprofiles.ku.dk/en/publications/is-there-a-correlation-between-androgens-and-sexual-desire-in-wom/). This represents a critical methodological finding: measurement innovation (moving from immunoassays to mass spectrometry quantification of primary metabolites) did not improve androgen-desire correlation strength, suggesting the problem is not measurement artifact but biological complexity.

---

## 2. Meta-Analytic Synthesis: Moderate Effects with Publication Bias

A systematic review and meta-analysis incorporating **34 studies with 3,268 women** [[11]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35227621/) provides quantified effect estimates but reveals important limitations through publication bias analysis.

### Primary Androgen Effect Sizes

| Androgen Metric | Effect Size (SMD) | 95% Confidence Interval | Statistical Significance | Clinical Interpretation |
|-----------------|-------------------|------------------------|--------------------------|------------------------|
| **Total Testosterone (TT)** | **0.59** | 0.29–0.88 | P < 0.0001 | Moderate positive association |
| **Free Testosterone/FAI** | Significant | — | P < 0.05 | Moderate positive association |
| **DHEA-S** | Positive association | — | P < 0.05 | Associated with global sexual function, not specifically sexual desire |

The **SMD of 0.59 for total testosterone** indicates a moderate effect size by Cohen's criteria (small ≥0.2, medium ≥0.5, large ≥0.8), translating to meaningful but not large associations. However, meta-analysis detected **significant publication bias**, suggesting that studies showing null or negative associations were under-represented in the literature [[11]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35227621/). This publication bias likely inflates the apparent effect sizes, indicating true population associations may be more modest than the pooled estimate suggests.

### Age-Dependent Associations in Meta-Analysis

Critical to understanding apparent contradictions: **associations between androgens and sexual desire systematically weaken with advancing age** [[11]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35227621/). This pattern aligns with the primary study's finding that older women (45–65 years) show fewer androgen correlations, suggesting age-related changes in androgen sensitivity, receptor expression, or psychological/relational factors increasingly dominate desire regulation with aging.

---

## 3. Premenopausal Women: The Inconsistency Crisis

A specialized systematic review focusing exclusively on **premenopausal women** (the population where androgen-desire mechanisms should theoretically be strongest due to stable ovulatory androgen production) found **surprisingly inconsistent evidence** [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf):

- **Testosterone serum studies**: 6 of 10 studies (**60%**) found **NO significant association** between serum testosterone and libido in premenopausal women [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf)
- **Total testosterone and sexuality**: 7 of 10 studies (**70%**) found total testosterone NOT related to sexual function [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf)
- **Treatment evidence**: Only 1 of 4 testosterone replacement studies in premenopausal women showed clear improvements, and notably, **only the intermediate dose (not the highest dose) achieved benefit in the Davis et al. study**, creating a paradox unexplained by simple dose-response relationships [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf)

This **60–70% null finding rate in premenopausal populations** directly contradicts both the meta-analysis moderate effect size and the impression from the primary study that robust correlations exist. The discrepancy likely reflects:
1. **Publication bias**: Null findings in premenopausal women underrepresented in literature [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf)
2. **Non-hormonal factors dominance**: In younger, partnered women, psychological, relational, and neurobiological factors may outweigh hormonal contributions
3. **Measurement sensitivity**: Baseline testosterone levels may be adequate for function in premenopausal women, making correlations with normal-range variation clinically insignificant

---

## 4. Natural Experiments: Mechanisms More Complex Than Receptor Binding

The strongest evidence that androgen-desire correlation is not universally applicable comes from **natural experiments where androgen-receptor signaling is either absent or markedly elevated** [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf).

### Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: High Androgens, Normal/Low Desire

Women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) produce **elevated androgens (testosterone 2–3× normal)** [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf). Clinical lore suggests these women should have enhanced sexual desire. However, research demonstrates women with PCOS presenting for antiandrogen therapy to treat hirsutism do **not report increased sexual desire** and treatment with antiandrogens (decreasing circulating androgens) **does not consistently decrease desire** [[16]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14504014/). This natural experiment reveals that **supraphysiological androgen elevation does not linearly increase sexual desire**, contradicting simple dose-response assumptions.

### Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome: No Functional Receptors, Preserved Libido

The most striking natural experiment involves women with **complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS)—individuals with XY karyotype, testes producing testosterone, but non-functional androgen receptors** [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf). Despite having circulating testosterone but completely blocked androgen receptor signaling:
- **71% reported average to strong sexual desire** [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf)
- **77% reported normal orgasm ability** [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf)

This demonstrates unequivocally that **androgen receptor signaling is not necessary for sexual desire development and expression**, revealing that alternative neural mechanisms can support normal libido independent of androgen signaling. The CAIS evidence indicates that estrogen (peripherally aromatized from testosterone), non-androgen neural mechanisms, or social/psychological factors can fully compensate for absent androgen signaling.

**Interpretation**: PCOS (high androgens, normal desire) and CAIS (no androgen receptors, normal desire) together prove that the androgen-desire relationship is **neither linearly dose-dependent nor absolutely necessary**, suggesting significant mediating factors.

---

## 5. The Clinical Efficacy Paradox: Therapy Works Despite Weak Correlations

Perhaps the most puzzling finding emerges from **testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) for hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD)**—therapy demonstrably improves sexual desire **despite weak baseline androgen-desire correlations**. This apparent paradox provides critical insight into mechanism.

### Randomized Controlled Trial Evidence

**Postmenopausal women with HSDD treated with transdermal testosterone** showed:
- **Increase in satisfying sexual episodes**: 2.1/month (testosterone) vs. 0.98/month (placebo), P < .001 [[1]](https://consultqd.clevelandclinic.org/the-role-of-androgen-therapy-in-female-sexual-health)
- **APHRODITE trial doses**: 300 μg/day (P < .001); 150 μg/day (P = .04) [[1]](https://consultqd.clevelandclinic.org/the-role-of-androgen-therapy-in-female-sexual-health)

**Meta-analysis across 36 randomized controlled trials (8,480 participants)** found **significant improvements in:**
- Sexual desire [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32205812/)
- Arousal [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32205812/)
- Orgasm [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32205812/)
- Pleasure [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32205812/)

**Timeline to clinical benefit**: Improvements observable at **6–8 weeks**; maximal benefit achieved at **12 weeks** [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf).

### The Paradox's Resolution

The efficacy paradox—that TRT works despite weak baseline correlations—can be resolved by distinguishing between:

1. **Baseline correlation significance**: Weak baseline associations suggest that in the general population, small variations in circulating androgens have modest effect on desire
2. **Therapeutic replacement effect**: Restoring androgens to physiologically normal levels after deficiency (surgical menopause, adrenal insufficiency, pituitary disease, age-related decline) may restore signaling above a threshold independent of baseline population correlations

**Clinical interpretation**: Androgens appear necessary for normal sexual desire function but not sufficient predictors of desire levels within the normal range. This distinction explains why clinical replacement works despite epidemiological correlations being modest.

---

## 6. Hormonal Contraceptive Confounding: The Relationship Obscured

Systemic hormonal contraceptive use represents a major confounder disrupting androgen-desire correlations by **suppressing ovarian androgen production**. This confounding is evident across multiple studies:

### Estradiol-Containing Contraceptives and Androgen Suppression

**Combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptives suppress androgen production** by:
- Decreasing 5-alpha reductase activity (reducing DHT formation) [[8]](https://www.redalyc.org/journal/817/81759552018/html/)
- Inhibiting dehydroepiandrosterone production [[8]](https://www.redalyc.org/journal/817/81759552018/html/)
- Decreasing testosterone and androstenedione [[8]](https://www.redalyc.org/journal/817/81759552018/html/)

### Sexual Desire Effects: Heterogeneous Outcomes

Despite documented androgen suppression, **sexual desire effects vary dramatically by formulation**:

| Contraceptive Formulation | Sexual Dysfunction Rate | Comparison | P-value |
|---------------------------|------------------------|------------|---------|
| **Ethinyl Estradiol (EE)-based** | **24.71%** | E2V/DNG | P < 0.01 [[8]](https://www.redalyc.org/journal/817/81759552018/html/) |
| **E2V (estradiol valerate)-based** | **9.41%** | EE-based | P < 0.01 [[8]](https://www.redalyc.org/journal/817/81759552018/html/) |
| Antiandrogenic pills (EE/DRSP) | **33%** arousal disorders | No contraception (8%) | — [[7]](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/dating-and-mating/202405/oral-contraceptives-may-inhibit-womens-sexual-desire) |
| **Most pill users overall** | **85% showed no change or improvement** | Baseline libido | — [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf) |

**Key finding**: Despite androgen suppression, **85% of women on oral contraceptives experience no libido change or improvement** [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf), suggesting that **androgen suppression does not universally decrease sexual desire** and may be offset by other hormonal or psychological mechanisms.

**Free Androgen Index (FAI) findings**: Women on ethinyl estradiol-containing pills showed the **lowest Free Androgen Index** and **lowest FSFI sexual desire scores**, with **statistically significant correlation between FAI and desire scores** [[9]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38588444/)—but this correlation is **observed within contraceptive-users only**, not in unmedicated women.

---

## 7. Measurement and Methodological Challenges

The evolution of androgen measurement from older immunoassays to modern liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) has revealed a **persistent measurement paradox**: newer methods with superior accuracy show **weaker** correlations with sexual desire than older methods, suggesting measurement artifact does not explain inconclusive correlations [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf).

### The Bioactive Testosterone Problem

Traditional total testosterone measurement includes both bioactive free testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG)-bound testosterone. However, **SHBG-bound testosterone is biologically inactive**, meaning total testosterone is an imprecise measure of physiologically relevant hormone. The primary study measured:
- Total testosterone (TT)
- Calculated free testosterone (FT)
- Androstenedione
- Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS)
- Androsterone glucuronide (ADT-G) [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/)

The finding that **calculated free testosterone correlates with desire while total testosterone shows weaker correlations in some subgroups** suggests **bioavailability is critical** [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/).

### The Intracrine Paradox

A major insight from recent research: **circulating androgens do not fully reflect tissue-level androgens**. Target tissues including the vagina synthesize androgens from precursor steroids (the "intracrine" pathway) [[6]](https://med-fom-brotto.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2014/12/Basson-Brotto-2010-Role-of-Androgens-2481.pdf). This means **serum measurements capture only one component of total androgen bioactivity**—possibly explaining why even sensitive LC-MS/MS measurements of circulating androgens show weak correlations. **Tissue androgen synthesis may be a better determinant of sexual function than circulating levels**, but this cannot be measured non-invasively in clinical practice.

---

## 8. Proposed Biological Mechanisms

Understanding why correlations are weak despite mechanism evidence requires examining how androgens regulate desire:

### Central Nervous System Mechanisms [[5]](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/50/7/10.31083/j.ceog5007141)

**Androgen receptor distribution and function:**
- Androgen receptors are concentrated in hypothalamus, preoptic area, amygdala, and hippocampus [[5]](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/50/7/10.31083/j.ceog5007141)
- Testosterone activates the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus, which stimulates olfactory and genital sensory centers [[5]](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/50/7/10.31083/j.ceog5007141)
- **Neurotransmitter modulation**: Androgens regulate dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), and neuropeptide signaling—all critical for desire initiation [[5]](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/50/7/10.31083/j.ceog5007141)

These multiple neural pathways and neurotransmitter systems suggest that androgens are **modulators of a complex neural system** rather than primary drivers, explaining why circulating androgen levels correlate weakly with functional sexual desire outcomes.

### Peripheral Mechanisms [[5]](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/50/7/10.31083/j.ceog5007141) [[6]](https://med-fom-brotto.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2014/12/Basson-Brotto-2010-Role-of-Androgens-2481.pdf)

**Vaginal tissue androgen synthesis:**
- Vaginal epithelium and supporting tissues contain 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase enzymes [[6]](https://med-fom-brotto.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2014/12/Basson-Brotto-2010-Role-of-Androgens-2481.pdf)
- These tissues synthesize dihydrotestosterone (DHT) from dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) locally [[6]](https://med-fom-brotto.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2014/12/Basson-Brotto-2010-Role-of-Androgens-2481.pdf)
- **Anti-inflammatory function**: DHT has anti-inflammatory effects on vaginal tissue, supporting genital arousal and pleasure sensations [[5]](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/50/7/10.31083/j.ceog5007141)

This intracrine pathway means that **inadequate precursor substrate (DHEA) availability could impair sexual function independent of circulating testosterone levels**, explaining why some androgens (DHEA, androstenedione) correlate better with desire than others in certain populations.

---

## 9. Age-Related Androgen Decline and Sexual Desire Trajectories

The **interplay between aging and androgens** explains much of the "inconclusive" overall correlation:

### Androgen Levels Across Life Stages

Both circulating androgens and sexual desire decline with advancing age. However, the relationship is **not perfectly concordant**:
- Testosterone declines approximately **0.8% per year** after age 30 in women [[15]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26176767/)
- Sexual desire declines but highly variable—some women maintain strong desire into advanced age [[15]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26176767/)

The dissociation between parallel androgen and desire declines (one more steep than the other in individual cases) suggests **multiple mechanisms regulate desire beyond androgens alone** [[15]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26176767/).

### Absence of Diagnostic Threshold

Critically, **no plasma androgen level cutoff exists that distinguishes sexual dysfunction from normal sexual function** [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf). This absence of a diagnostic threshold for any androgen concentration demonstrates that circulating androgen levels alone cannot determine whether sexual desire is normal or pathologic—confounders and context determine clinical presentation.

---

## 10. Clinical Applications and Safety Profile

Despite inconclusive correlations, testosterone therapy for HSDD has established clinical efficacy with a documented safety profile:

### FDA and Regulatory Approval Status

- **United States**: No FDA-approved female-specific testosterone formulation; **estimated 2 million+ off-label prescriptions annually** [[4]](https://downloads.regulations.gov/FDA-2025-N-2589-0383/attachment_1.pdf)
- **Australia**: AndroFeme® approved **November 2020**; **4.5 years of real-world data documenting 2 adverse events** [[4]](https://downloads.regulations.gov/FDA-2025-N-2589-0383/attachment_1.pdf)
- **New Zealand**: AndroFeme® 1 approved **April 2025** [[10]](https://www.goodfellowunit.org/medcases/female-sexual-dysfunction-place-testosterone)

This regulatory divergence reflects ongoing debate about the evidence strength for female androgen replacement.

### Short-Term Safety Profile (≤24 months)

Meta-analyses and systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials document the following safety profile:

| Adverse Event | Incidence (TRT) | Incidence (Placebo) | Clinical Significance |
|---------------|-----------------|-------------------|----------------------|
| **Acne** | 7.5% | 5.0% | Mild; reversible |
| **Hirsutism** | 8.6% | 6.1% | Cosmetic concern; manageable |
| **Cardiovascular events** | —— | —— | 4-year trial, 3,656 women, >7,300 woman-years: **53 cardiovascular events LOWER than expected baseline** [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf) |
| **Breast cancer/density** | No increased density | —— | Rates consistent with age-related background; **no signal of increased risk** [[10]](https://www.goodfellowunit.org/medcases/female-sexual-dysfunction-place-testosterone) |

The cardiovascular safety finding is particularly reassuring: a large trial with >7,300 woman-years of follow-up documented **fewer cardiovascular events than epidemiologically expected**, suggesting no adverse cardiovascular effect or potential protective effect [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf).

### Long-Term Safety Data Limitations

**Data beyond 24 months is limited**, representing a recognized gap in the evidence base [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf). All current recommendations note that long-term safety (beyond 2 years) remains inconclusive and requires continued monitoring.

---

## 11. Integrative Analysis: Why the Answer is "MAYBE"

The evidence comprehensively demonstrates that the androgen-sexual desire relationship is **genuinely inconclusive when examined across all populations and contexts**, yet specific subpopulations show clear correlations. This nuanced answer ("maybe") reflects the data more accurately than simple yes/no responses:

### Evidence Supporting "YES" (Correlations Exist)

1. **Moderate meta-analytic associations**: SMD 0.59 (P < 0.0001) for total testosterone across 34 studies [[11]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35227621/)
2. **Primary study correlations in specific populations**: FT and androstenedione correlate in total cohort; TT, FT, androstenedione, DHEAS correlate in younger contraceptive-naive women [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/)
3. **Therapeutic efficacy**: Testosterone replacement improves sexual desire and arousal in HSDD (P < .001) [[1]](https://consultqd.clevelandclinic.org/the-role-of-androgen-therapy-in-female-sexual-health) [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32205812/)
4. **Mechanistic evidence**: Established androgen receptor expression in sexual desire neural circuits [[5]](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/50/7/10.31083/j.ceog5007141)

### Evidence Supporting "NO" (Correlations Absent or Inconsistent)

1. **Premenopausal systematic review**: 60% of testosterone serum studies found NO correlation; 70% found total testosterone not related to sexuality [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf)
2. **Publication bias in meta-analysis**: Reported associations inflated by underrepresentation of null findings [[11]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35227621/)
3. **Natural experiments**: PCOS (elevated androgens, normal desire); CAIS (no functional androgen receptors, normal desire) [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf)
4. **Hormonal contraceptive paradox**: 85% of pill users experience no change or improvement in desire despite androgen suppression [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf)
5. **Absence of diagnostic threshold**: No androgen level predicts dysfunction [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf)

### Evidence Supporting "INCONCLUSIVE" (Context Dependency)

1. **Inconclusive abstract statement** from primary study [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/)
2. **Age-dependent associations**: Strong in ages 25–44, weak in ages 45–65 [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/)
3. **Measurement inadequacy**: No biomarker perfectly predicts sexual desire; intracrine androgen synthesis unmeasured [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf) [[6]](https://med-fom-brotto.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2014/12/Basson-Brotto-2010-Role-of-Androgens-2481.pdf)
4. **Multifactorial sexual desire**: Psychological, relational, neurobiological, and hormonal factors all contribute; androgens alone insufficient [[5]](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/CEOG/50/7/10.31083/j.ceog5007141)
5. **Therapy-correlation dissociation**: Clinical efficacy despite weak baseline correlations [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf)

---

## 12. Conclusion: Context-Dependent Correlations in Specific Populations

The scientific evidence unequivocally demonstrates that **androgens and sexual desire in women are correlated in some populations under specific conditions**, yet correlations are **absent, weak, or confounded in many other populations**. The following synthesis captures the evidence:

**In young, healthy, non-contraceptive-using women aged 25–44**, androgens (particularly free testosterone, androstenedione, and DHEAS) show **statistically significant positive correlations with sexual desire** [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/). This population demonstrates that the mechanism linking androgens to desire is physiologically real and measurable.

**In older women aged 45–65**, androgen-desire correlations weaken dramatically, with only androstenedione remaining significantly correlated, suggesting **age-related changes in androgen sensitivity, receptor expression, or increasing dominance of non-hormonal factors** [[12]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25475395/).

**In premenopausal women broadly**, 60–70% of studies find **no significant correlation** between circulating androgens and sexual function, indicating that **in reproductive-age women with physiologically normal androgens, small variations in circulating levels are poor predictors of sexual desire** [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf).

**Natural experiments** (PCOS: elevated androgens with normal desire; CAIS: absent androgen receptors with normal desire) prove that androgens are **neither linearly dose-dependent nor absolutely necessary** for sexual desire [[17]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2e14/9865ca9df4bd5d084437dc6d1b9983a8fc92.pdf).

**Testosterone replacement therapy efficacy** (despite weak baseline correlations) suggests androgens function as **modulators of sexual desire above a threshold rather than direct determinants across the physiological range** [[3]](https://www.isswsh.org/images/PDF/jsm_18_5_849.pdf).

The **intrinsic complexity** of sexual desire regulation—involving dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline, GABA, neuropeptides, relationship quality, psychological state, partner availability, health status, medication side effects, and intracrine tissue androgen synthesis—explains why **circulating androgen measurements capture only one determinant of a multifactorial process**.

**Therefore, the most scientifically accurate answer to "Is there a correlation between androgens and sexual desire in women?" is MAYBE.** Yes, clear correlations exist in specific subpopulations (particularly young, non-medicated women). No, these correlations are not universal, predictive, or sufficient to establish diagnostic or prognostic cutoffs. Inconclusive overall because context, age, medication, and unmeasured tissue-level androgen synthesis significantly modulate observable correlations. The relationship is real but nuanced, mediated by multiple systems, and only partially explained by circulating androgen concentrations alone.

question: Human papillomavirus and pterygium. Is the virus a risk factor?
context:
Pterygium is a disease of unknown origin and pathogenesis that might be vision threatening. It is characterised by a wing-like conjunctival overgrowth of the cornea. Several studies have investigated human papillomavirus (HPV) as a risk factor for the development of pterygia, but the results are inconclusive.AIM: To investigate a large sample of pterygia for the presence of HPV in order to clarify the putative association between pterygia and HPV.

100 specimens of pterygium from Danish patients and 20 normal conjunctival biopsy specimens were investigated for the presence of HPV with PCR technique using beta-globin primers to access the quality of the extracted DNA and the HPV primers MY09/11 and GP5+/6+. HPV-positive specimens underwent subsequent HPV typing with type-specific HPV primers and further investigation with DNA in situ hybridisation (ISH).

90 of 100 investigated pterygia proved suitable for HPV analysis by PCR. As beta-globin could not be amplified, 10 specimens were excluded from the study. 4 of 90 pterygia harboured HPV. HPV type 6 was identified in all four HPV-positive pterygia. The 20 normal conjunctival biopsy specimens were beta-globin positive and HPV negative. All four pterygia that were HPV type 6 positive were DNA ISH negative.
long_answer: The low presence of HPV DNA in pterygia does not support the hypothesis that HPV is involved in the development of pterygia in Denmark.

Pterygium is a disease of unknown origin and pathogenesis that might be vision threatening. It is characterised by a wing-like conjunctival overgrowth of the cornea. Several studies have investigated human papillomavirus (HPV) as a risk factor for the development of pterygia, but the results are inconclusive.AIM: To investigate a large sample of pterygia for the presence of HPV in order to clarify the putative association between pterygia and HPV.
