## Diagnostic Criteria: Ensuring Proper Patient Selection

The efficacy of multimodal cervical physical therapy depends critically on accurate diagnosis of cervicogenic somatic tinnitus. Case studies reported positive treatment effects in tinnitus cases with cervical involvement, but without rigorous selection criteria, treatment outcomes would be heterogeneous. [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/)

**Established Diagnostic Criteria:** Michiels and colleagues developed a standardized diagnostic framework through a Delphi consensus process, establishing four required criteria for CST diagnosis: [[1]](https://repository.uantwerpen.be/docman/irua/112d67/129906.pdf) [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26045606/)

1. **Neck pain** (active or chronic musculoskeletal neck dysfunction)
2. **Impaired cervical range of motion**, preferably rotational limitation (indicating mechanical dysfunction)
3. **Modulation of tinnitus by head/neck movements and/or posture** (demonstrating somatosensory-auditory coupling)
4. **Tenderness of cervical-occipital muscles** (identifying the source of nociceptive input)

The requirement that **all four criteria must be present** prevents misclassification of tinnitus cases with incidental neck complaints as cervicogenic in origin.

**Validated Diagnostic Tests:** Clinical examination tests have established diagnostic utility for CST:

- **Manual rotation test:** Likelihood ratio (LR) of **5**, specificity **90%**, resulting in post-test probability of **78%** when positive. [[9]](https://www.londonspine.com/diagnostic-value-of-clinical-cervical-spine-tests-in-patients-with-cervicogenic-somatic-tinnitus/) [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26045606/) This test assesses whether cervical rotation modulates tinnitus perception.

- **Adapted Spurling Test:** Identical diagnostic characteristics—LR **5**, specificity **90%**, post-test probability **78%**. [[9]](https://www.londonspine.com/diagnostic-value-of-clinical-cervical-spine-tests-in-patients-with-cervicogenic-somatic-tinnitus/) [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26045606/)

- **Neck Bournemouth Questionnaire (NBQ) score <14:** Sensitivity **80%**, LR **0.3**, post-test probability **19%**. [[9]](https://www.londonspine.com/diagnostic-value-of-clinical-cervical-spine-tests-in-patients-with-cervicogenic-somatic-tinnitus/) [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26045606/) An NBQ score below 14 effectively excludes CST, given the intrinsic link between neck dysfunction and cervicogenic tinnitus.

- **Absence of cervical trigger points:** Sensitivity **82%**, LR **0.3**, post-test probability **22%** when absent. [[9]](https://www.londonspine.com/diagnostic-value-of-clinical-cervical-spine-tests-in-patients-with-cervicogenic-somatic-tinnitus/) [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26045606/) The absence of cervical muscle trigger points argues against a myofascial contribution to tinnitus.

These diagnostic tests enable clinicians to differentiate CST—which responds well to cervical rehabilitation—from tinnitus of purely audiologic origin (sensorineural hearing loss, noise-induced trauma) or central origin (brainstem/cortical pathology), which would not be expected to respond to cervical physical therapy. [[11]](https://www.entandaudiologynews.com/features/audiology-features/post/diagnosing-and-managing-somatic-tinnitus)

## Treatment Components and Intervention Intensity

Efficacy depends not only on correct patient selection but also on comprehensive, multimodal treatment delivery. The evidence base identifies specific intervention components and optimal treatment intensity.

**Manual Therapy Component:** Cervical and thoracic mobilizations form the manual foundation. These include rotational mobilizations to restore cervical segmental mobility, lateral glide techniques to address facet joint restrictions, and postero-anterior (PA) glides to mobilize vertebral segments and associated musculature. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) techniques—including distraction, glides, and direct muscle release—address the trigeminocervical convergence zone and reduce afferent trigeminal nociception contributing to DCN disinhibition. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Soft tissue mobilization and myofascial release techniques address muscle tension and trigger point activity that amplify cervical nociception. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf)

**Exercise Prescription:** The exercise program emphasizes both flexibility restoration and neuromuscular control. Stretching targets muscles commonly restricted in cervicogenic conditions: axial extension movements, pectoralis major and minor, upper trapezius, levator scapulae, and sternocleidomastoid. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Deep neck flexor recruitment—the cervical analogues of core stabilization in spinal rehabilitation—is integrated with functional upper extremity movements, training coordinated stabilization during daily activities. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Progressive cervical stabilization exercises build endurance of deep cervical muscles, reducing reliance on pain-amplifying superficial muscle patterns. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Supplementary strengthening targets the temporomandibular joint, upper extremity, and thoracic girdle to restore force couple balance around the cervical spine and jaw. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf)

**Postural Intervention:** Postural coaching and ergonomic education identify and correct biomechanical abnormalities perpetuating cervical dysfunction. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Forward head posture, rounded shoulders, and desk-based positioning abnormalities are addressed through specific postural retraining and workstation modification.

**Treatment Intensity and Dosage:** The evidence suggests specific intensity parameters optimize outcomes. Studies employed **2-3 sessions per week for 4-7 weeks** in 60-minute treatment sessions. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Within these parameters, data comparing improved versus unimproved patients revealed a notable intensity difference: patients achieving tinnitus improvement averaged **11.4 ± 2.6 treatments**, while those without improvement completed **9.5 ± 2.5 treatments** (p = 0.049). [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) This finding suggests that more intensive treatment exposure—approaching the higher end of the range—may enhance therapeutic benefit, though individual variation in treatment response remains substantial.

## Outcome Measures and Clinical Significance

Proper interpretation of treatment efficacy requires understanding the outcome measures employed and their clinical meaning thresholds.

**Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI):** The primary measure in the RCT, the TFI is a 25-item self-report questionnaire scored on a 0-100 scale, with higher scores reflecting greater functional impairment from tinnitus. [[7]](https://www.ncrar.research.va.gov/Education/Documents/TinnitusDocuments/TFI_EarHearing_2011.pdf) [[8]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22156949/) The scale stratifies severity as follows: **TFI <25** indicates mild tinnitus with minimal functional impact; **TFI 25-50** represents significant tinnitus problems potentially warranting intervention; **TFI >50** indicates severe tinnitus-related handicap requiring aggressive treatment consideration. [[7]](https://www.ncrar.research.va.gov/Education/Documents/TinnitusDocuments/TFI_EarHearing_2011.pdf) The TFI demonstrates strong validity and responsiveness to treatment-related change, making it suitable for both clinical and research applications. [[8]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22156949/) The **Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) for TFI is a 13-point reduction**, [[6]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38351518/) [[7]](https://www.ncrar.research.va.gov/Education/Documents/TinnitusDocuments/TFI_EarHearing_2011.pdf) meaning that a change of 13 points or greater on the TFI represents a meaningful difference to patients beyond statistical noise. The RCT's finding of significant TFI reduction (p = 0.04) indicates that cervical physical therapy achieves clinically detectable tinnitus improvement.

**Neck Bournemouth Questionnaire (NBQ):** This measure quantifies neck-related disability and functional limitation. The trial's highly significant NBQ reduction (p < 0.001) demonstrates substantial improvement in neck dysfunction accompanying tinnitus improvement, suggesting that the pathophysiological link between cervical dysfunction and tinnitus is reversible through rehabilitation.

**Additional Outcome Measures:** Supporting studies employed the **Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI)**, a 25-item measure of tinnitus-related handicap across emotional, functional, and catastrophic domains. [[15]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2016.00545/full) The **Visual Analog Scale (VAS)** measured subjective tinnitus loudness and annoyance on continuous scales, providing simple but sensitive tinnitus perception data. [[15]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2016.00545/full) The **Global Perceived Effect (GPE)** scale captured patient-reported overall improvement trajectories—the measure that identified **53% substantial improvement** immediately post-treatment in the RCT. [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/)

## Clinical Prognostic Factors for Treatment Success

Not all CST patients respond equally to multimodal cervical physical therapy. Identification of baseline characteristics predicting treatment response enables risk stratification and treatment planning.

**Favorable Prognostic Indicators:** A study examining prognostic factors in cervical physical therapy for somatic tinnitus identified baseline characteristics associated with favorable treatment response: [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf)

- **No increase in tinnitus with noise exposure:** Patients whose tinnitus does not worsen in response to acoustic stimuli demonstrate better treatment outcomes, suggesting somatosensory dominance over auditory pathology.

- **Absence of family history of tinnitus:** Patients without familial tinnitus ancestry show better responses, potentially reflecting reduced contribution of genetic predisposition to tinnitus severity.

- **Recent tinnitus onset:** Patients with shorter symptom duration respond more favorably, consistent with neuroplasticity principles suggesting that chronic tinnitus-related central sensitization is harder to reverse than recently developed tinnitus.

- **Demonstrated somatosensory modulation ability:** Patients whose tinnitus can be modulated (increased or decreased) through neck movements and posture demonstrate the clearest evidence of cervicogenic contribution and show the best treatment outcomes. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf)

These prognostic factors serve dual purposes: they refine the diagnosis of CST (by requiring demonstrated tinnitus modulation) and identify subgroups likely to achieve clinical benefit, enabling more honest prognostication with patients considering treatment.

## Mechanistic Understanding: Why Cervical Therapy Works

The clinical efficacy of cervical physical therapy for CST is not merely empirical; substantial neuroscientific evidence explains the underlying mechanisms, providing confidence that observed improvements reflect genuine pathophysiological modulation rather than placebo effect.

**Dorsal Cochlear Nucleus Convergence:** The DCN receives dual sensory input from auditory and cervical somatosensory sources. Proprioceptive signals from intact cervical mechanoreceptors normally inhibit DCN neuronal activity, maintaining appropriate tinnitus perception thresholds. [[1]](https://repository.uantwerpen.be/docman/irua/112d67/129906.pdf) When cervical pathology (disc herniation, facet osteoarthritis, muscle dysfunction) generates nociceptive and aberrant proprioceptive signals, these converge at the DCN, causing neural disinhibition—a state of reduced suppression of spontaneous DCN activity, amplifying tinnitus perception. [[1]](https://repository.uantwerpen.be/docman/irua/112d67/129906.pdf) Manual therapy and exercise restore normal proprioceptive input architecture and reduce nociceptive afferent traffic, re-establishing inhibitory tone at the DCN and suppressing tinnitus. [[1]](https://repository.uantwerpen.be/docman/irua/112d67/129906.pdf) [[4]](https://drbillgrubbsblog.com/2137/the-cervical-spine-and-tinnitus/)

**Trigeminal-Cervical Nucleus Convergence:** The trigeminal cervical nucleus in the brainstem receives overlapping inputs from cranial nerve V (trigeminal) and upper cervical spinal nerves (C1-C4). [[4]](https://drbillgrubbsblog.com/2137/the-cervical-spine-and-tinnitus/) This anatomical convergence zone enables trigeminal (jaw/facial) and cervical musculoskeletal pathology to interact in driving tinnitus. Treatment addressing both cervical spine dysfunction and associated TMJ dysfunction via the multimodal protocol optimizes this convergence zone management. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf)

**Neuroplastic Restoration:** The trigeminal-cervical complex undergoes reorganization in chronic tinnitus, with expanded receptive fields and altered gain of sensory inputs. [[4]](https://drbillgrubbsblog.com/2137/the-cervical-spine-and-tinnitus/) Progressive cervical rehabilitation, through sustained proprioceptive normalization and motor retraining, gradually restores organized receptive field geometry and appropriate neural gain, reversing some aspects of tinnitus-related central sensitization. [[1]](https://repository.uantwerpen.be/docman/irua/112d67/129906.pdf) The observation that **45% of treated patients maintained improvement at follow-up** while **53% showed immediate improvement** suggests that while acute disinhibition reduction occurs during treatment, sustained reversal of neuroplastic changes requires continued practice and proprioceptive maintenance. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf)

## Limitations and Long-Term Outcomes: Critical Considerations

While the evidence for cervical physical therapy improving CST is substantial, important limitations warrant acknowledgment.

**Sustainability Challenge:** The most clinically significant limitation concerns durability of benefit. The RCT documented **53% substantial improvement immediately post-treatment** but only **24% maintained substantial improvement at 6-week follow-up**—a **55% decline in maintenance rate** in the short term. [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/) This pattern suggests that acute treatment effects on CST-related tinnitus may require maintenance therapy, periodic "booster" sessions, or continued home exercise practice to prevent symptom recurrence. The mechanisms underlying this decline—whether reflecting neuroplastic recurrence without continued proprioceptive input, inadequate home exercise adherence, or biomechanical reversion without ongoing postural awareness—remain incompletely characterized in available literature.

**Study Quality Considerations:** While the primary RCT is well-designed and the systematic review's inclusion of six positive studies is encouraging, the systematic review acknowledged moderate-to-high bias risk in individual studies, primarily due to inherent blinding challenges in manual therapy research. [[15]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2016.00545/full) The difficulty of creating convincing sham manual therapy treatments introduces placebo uncertainty—patients cannot be truly blinded to whether they received genuine versus sham manipulation. This limitation affects effect size interpretation but does not negate the clinical meaningfulness of observed improvements.

**Limited Long-Term Data:** The RCT and supporting studies provide follow-up data through **6 weeks post-treatment**. [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/) [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Data beyond this timeframe—examining 3-month, 6-month, or 1-year outcomes—are limited in the published literature. Understanding whether treatment benefits persist, plateau, or decline over longer durations would inform treatment planning and patient expectations more completely.

**Heterogeneity in Treatment Response:** While prognostic factors have been identified, substantial individual variation in treatment response persists. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Not all patients meeting diagnostic criteria achieve improvement; baseline prognostic indicators predict but do not guarantee outcomes. This heterogeneity likely reflects unmeasured biological factors, compliance differences, or uncontrolled variables affecting treatment effectiveness.

## Clinical Application: Integrating Evidence into Practice

The cumulative evidence supports recommending multimodal cervical physical therapy as an evidence-based intervention for patients with properly diagnosed cervicogenic somatic tinnitus. However, optimal implementation requires structured integration:

**Patient Selection:** Candidates should meet all four diagnostic criteria (neck pain, restricted cervical ROM, tinnitus modulation by movement, cervical muscle tenderness) and score >14 on the Neck Bournemouth Questionnaire. [[1]](https://repository.uantwerpen.be/docman/irua/112d67/129906.pdf) [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26045606/) Patients with favorable prognostic indicators—recent symptom onset, demonstrated tinnitus modulation, absence of family history, and noise-unresponsive tinnitus—are more likely to achieve substantial improvement. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf)

**Treatment Expectations:** Patients should expect significant tinnitus improvement in the immediate post-treatment period (53% achieve substantial improvement), [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/) but understand that this improvement may not persist without maintenance strategies. [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/) Setting realistic expectations about the **24% maintenance rate at 6 weeks** prevents disappointment and encourages continued engagement with home exercise and postural management.

**Treatment Protocol:** A **6-week intensive program of 12 sessions** (approximately 2 sessions weekly) combining manual therapy, progressive cervical exercise, and postural education represents the evidence-supported standard. [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/) [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf) Clinicians should individualize intensity within the framework of **2-3 sessions per week for 4-7 weeks** to optimize benefit, with more intensive protocols (approaching 11.4 average treatments) correlating with better outcomes. [[14]](https://www.thieme-connect.com/products/ejournals/pdf/10.3766/jaaa.17147.pdf)

**Maintenance Planning:** Post-treatment maintenance should include prescribed home exercise progression, periodic postural retraining, and consideration of periodic "booster" sessions to sustain improvements, given the observed decline in maintenance rates between immediate post-treatment and 6-week follow-up. [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/)

## Conclusion

Multimodal cervical physical therapy demonstrably improves tinnitus in properly selected patients with cervicogenic somatic tinnitus. This conclusion rests on multiple sources of evidence: a well-designed randomized controlled trial showing statistically significant TFI improvement and **53% substantial clinical improvement rates**; [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/) a comprehensive systematic review demonstrating consistent positive effects across **six independent studies**; [[15]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2016.00545/full) established pathophysiological mechanisms explaining how cervical rehabilitation modulates auditory perception; [[1]](https://repository.uantwerpen.be/docman/irua/112d67/129906.pdf) [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39188460/) [[4]](https://drbillgrubbsblog.com/2137/the-cervical-spine-and-tinnitus/) and validated diagnostic criteria enabling accurate patient selection. [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26045606/) [[11]](https://www.entandaudiologynews.com/features/audiology-features/post/diagnosing-and-managing-somatic-tinnitus)

The intervention is multimodal, combining manual therapy, progressive exercise, and postural education, and produces substantial acute effects. However, clinicians and patients must recognize that while immediate post-treatment improvement rates are encouraging, long-term sustainability of benefit requires attention, with only **24% maintaining substantial improvement at 6-week follow-up**. [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27592038/) This pattern indicates that cervicogenic somatic tinnitus may require sustained management rather than a single course of therapy.

For the specific population—patients with concurrent severe subjective tinnitus and neck complaints meeting all diagnostic criteria—multimodal cervical physical therapy represents a first-line, evidence-supported intervention with favorable safety profiles and clear mechanisms of action.

sources.snippet: Cervicogenic somatic tinnitus (CST) is a subgroup of somatosensory tinnitus that arises from altered sensory input from the cervical spine due to changes in anatomical and physiological functions. Unlike primary tinnitus, usually caused by auditory system issues, CST is due to somatosensory disruptions from the cervical region. Conditions such as degenerative disc disease, cervical spondylosis, whiplash injuries, and neck muscle stress or spasms are commonly associated with CST. The pathophysiology of CST involves complex interactions between the cervical spine’s somatosensory inputs and central auditory pathways, particularly affecting the dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN) in the brainstem, leading to enhanced excitability and synaptic reorganization, giving rise to tinnitus. Accurate diagnosis and management of CST require a comprehensive approach, including patient history, physical examination, audiological assessments, and imaging studies. Treatment strategies encompass physical therapy, medications, interventional procedures, and complementary therapies, aiming to reduce tinnitus perception, alleviate neck dysfunction, and improve overall quality of life. Emerging therapies, such as neuromodulation and regenerative medicine, show promise in further improving CST management. This multidisciplinary approach highlights the importance of addressing both musculoskeletal and auditory health in the effective treatment of CST.

question: Detailed analysis of sputum and systemic inflammation in asthma phenotypes: are paucigranulocytic asthmatics really non-inflammatory?
context:
The technique of induced sputum has allowed to subdivide asthma patients into inflammatory phenotypes according to their level of granulocyte airway infiltration. There are very few studies which looked at detailed sputum and blood cell counts in a large cohort of asthmatics divided into inflammatory phenotypes. The purpose of this study was to analyze sputum cell counts, blood leukocytes and systemic inflammatory markers in these phenotypes, and investigate how those groups compared with healthy subjects.

We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study on 833 asthmatics recruited from the University Asthma Clinic of Liege and compared them with 194 healthy subjects. Asthmatics were classified into inflammatory phenotypes.

The total non-squamous cell count per gram of sputum was greater in mixed granulocytic and neutrophilic phenotypes as compared to eosinophilic, paucigranulocytic asthma and healthy subjects (p < 0.005). Sputum eosinophils (in absolute values and percentages) were increased in all asthma phenotypes including paucigranulocytic asthma, compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005). Eosinophilic asthma showed higher absolute sputum neutrophil and lymphocyte counts than healthy subjects (p < 0.005), while neutrophilic asthmatics had a particularly low number of sputum macrophages and epithelial cells. All asthma phenotypes showed an increased blood leukocyte count compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005), with paucigranulocytic asthmatics having also increased absolute blood eosinophils compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005). Neutrophilic asthma had raised CRP and fibrinogen while eosinophilic asthma only showed raised fibrinogen compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005).
long_answer: This study demonstrates that a significant eosinophilic inflammation is present across all categories of asthma, and that paucigranulocytic asthma may be seen as a low grade inflammatory disease.

Question:
Detailed analysis of sputum and systemic inflammation in asthma phenotypes: are paucigranulocytic asthmatics really non-inflammatory?

PubMed abstract context:
The technique of induced sputum has allowed to subdivide asthma patients into inflammatory phenotypes according to their level of granulocyte airway infiltration. There are very few studies which looked at detailed sputum and blood cell counts in a large cohort of asthmatics divided into inflammatory phenotypes. The purpose of this study was to analyze sputum cell counts, blood leukocytes and systemic inflammatory markers in these phenotypes, and investigate how those groups compared with healthy subjects.

We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study on 833 asthmatics recruited from the University Asthma Clinic of Liege and compared them with 194 healthy subjects. Asthmatics were classified into inflammatory phenotypes.

The total non-squamous cell count per gram of sputum was greater in mixed granulocytic and neutrophilic phenotypes as compared to eosinophilic, paucigranulocytic asthma and healthy subjects (p < 0.005). Sputum eosinophils (in absolute values and percentages) were increased in all asthma phenotypes including paucigranulocytic asthma, compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005). Eosinophilic asthma showed higher absolute sputum neutrophil and lymphocyte counts than healthy subjects (p < 0.005), while neutrophilic asthmatics had a particularly low number of sputum macrophages and epithelial cells. All asthma phenotypes showed an increased blood leukocyte count compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005), with paucigranulocytic asthmatics having also increased absolute blood eosinophils compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005). Neutrophilic asthma had raised CRP and fibrinogen while eosinophilic asthma only showed raised fibrinogen compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005).

final_text:
# Paucigranulocytic Asthma: Evidence Against the "Non-Inflammatory" Designation

## Executive Summary

Despite their classification as "paucigranulocytic," asthmatics with this phenotype exhibit measurable low-grade airway and systemic inflammation that distinguishes them from healthy controls. A large retrospective cross-sectional study of **833 asthmatics compared with 194 healthy subjects** at the University Asthma Clinic of Liege demonstrated that paucigranulocytic asthmatics have elevated sputum eosinophils (both absolute values and percentages), increased blood leukocyte counts, and elevated absolute blood eosinophils when compared to healthy controls [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/). While these patients show lower inflammatory cell counts relative to other asthma phenotypes, the absence of high granulocytic infiltration does not equate to absence of inflammation. The evidence indicates that paucigranulocytic asthma represents a **low-grade inflammatory disease** [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf) driven by non-classical inflammatory mechanisms including mast cell activation, airway smooth muscle remodeling, and neurogenic pathways, rather than a truly non-inflammatory condition.

## Introduction: Classification of Asthma Phenotypes by Inflammatory Profile

Asthma has emerged as a heterogeneous disease characterized by multiple distinct inflammatory phenotypes that can be identified through induced sputum analysis. The technique of induced sputum allows clinicians and researchers to subdivide asthma patients into inflammatory phenotypes based on their level of granulocyte airway infiltration [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/). These phenotypes typically include eosinophilic asthma, neutrophilic asthma, mixed granulocytic asthma, and paucigranulocytic asthma.

The paucigranulocytic phenotype is defined by sputum eosinophils **less than 3% and sputum neutrophils less than 61-64%**, representing the lowest granulocytic infiltration pattern [[1]](https://www.heraldopenaccess.us/openaccess/clinical-features-and-management-of-neutrophilic-asthma) [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28407269/). This phenotype is notably the most common inflammatory subtype observed in stable asthma populations, comprising approximately **47.9% of 240 patients** in one comprehensive cohort analysis, with prevalence ranging from **33.3% to 52%** across different studies [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28407269/) [[1]](https://www.heraldopenaccess.us/openaccess/clinical-features-and-management-of-neutrophilic-asthma) [[8]](https://www.dovepress.com/characteristics-of-induced-sputum-inflammatory-phenotypes-in-adults-wi-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-JAA). In contrast, eosinophilic asthma represents 40-50% of patients, neutrophilic asthma occurs in 5-15.6% of cases, and mixed granulocytic asthma affects 4-6.7% of the asthma population [[1]](https://www.heraldopenaccess.us/openaccess/clinical-features-and-management-of-neutrophilic-asthma) [[8]](https://www.dovepress.com/characteristics-of-induced-sputum-inflammatory-phenotypes-in-adults-wi-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-JAA) [[9]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2022.969243/full).

The term "paucigranulocytic" literally refers to the low (though not absent) granulocytic cell count characteristic of the phenotype. The critical question addressed by contemporary research is whether this low granulocytic profile truly indicates a non-inflammatory condition or represents a distinct pattern of inflammation driven by alternative pathophysiological mechanisms.

## Methodological Framework of the Primary Evidence

The definitive study addressing this question employed a robust research design examining detailed sputum and blood inflammation markers across asthma phenotypes. The investigation was a **retrospective cross-sectional study** conducted on **833 asthmatics** recruited from the University Asthma Clinic of Liege, with comparison to **194 healthy subjects** [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/). Participants were stratified into inflammatory phenotypes based on their induced sputum cell counts, enabling comparison of sputum cell profiles, blood leukocyte counts, and systemic inflammatory markers across groups.

The use of induced sputum analysis represents the gold standard for identifying airway inflammatory phenotypes, as it directly measures the cellular composition of the lower airways and provides both absolute and percentage values for granulocytes and other inflammatory cells. The inclusion of a healthy control group enabled assessment of whether paucigranulocytic asthmatics differed from truly non-inflammatory individuals.

## Sputum Inflammation: Evidence of Persistent Eosinophilic Infiltration

The most striking finding regarding the inflammatory status of paucigranulocytic asthma emerged from analysis of sputum eosinophil counts. **Sputum eosinophils (measured in both absolute values and percentages) were increased in ALL asthma phenotypes, including paucigranulocytic asthma, when compared to healthy subjects, with statistical significance (p < 0.005)** [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/). This finding is critical because it demonstrates that even asthmatics classified as "paucigranulocytic"—a designation based on low overall granulocyte counts—nonetheless exhibit elevated eosinophilic inflammation relative to healthy controls.

The total non-squamous cell count per gram of sputum demonstrated phenotype-specific patterns. **This measure was greater in mixed granulocytic and neutrophilic phenotypes compared to eosinophilic asthma, paucigranulocytic asthma, and healthy subjects (p < 0.005)** [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/). Thus, while paucigranulocytic asthmatics show lower overall sputum cellularity than neutrophilic and mixed phenotypes, they still exceed the inflammatory burden observed in healthy controls.

When examining individual cell types within the sputum, eosinophilic asthma demonstrated **higher absolute sputum neutrophil and lymphocyte counts compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005)** [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/), indicating that multi-phenotypic granulocytic involvement characterizes certain asthma subtypes. Conversely, **neutrophilic asthmatics exhibited particularly low numbers of sputum macrophages and epithelial cells** [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/), suggesting phenotype-specific patterns of cellular composition that extend beyond simple granulocyte enumeration.

## Systemic Inflammatory Markers: Evidence of Blood-Based Inflammation

Beyond the airways, systemic inflammation measured through blood analysis provided additional evidence of inflammatory activity in paucigranulocytic asthma. **All asthma phenotypes showed an increased blood leukocyte count compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005)** [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/). This finding indicates that regardless of sputum phenotype classification, asthmatics exhibit systemic immunological activation relative to health.

Most importantly for paucigranulocytic asthma specifically, **paucigranulocytic asthmatics had increased absolute blood eosinophils compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005)** [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/). This finding directly contradicts the notion that paucigranulocytic asthmatics lack eosinophilic inflammation; rather, their blood eosinophil levels are elevated despite their low airway eosinophilic infiltration. This pattern suggests compartmentalization of the inflammatory response, with systemic eosinophilic activation persisting despite limited airway recruitment in this phenotype.

Acute phase reactants, the systemic proteins elevated in response to inflammatory stimuli, demonstrated a phenotype-specific pattern. **Neutrophilic asthma showed raised C-reactive protein (CRP) and fibrinogen levels compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005), while eosinophilic asthma exhibited raised fibrinogen only compared to healthy subjects (p < 0.005)** [[3]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27044366/). While the primary study did not separately detail CRP and fibrinogen values for the paucigranulocytic group in the abstract provided, the elevation of these biomarkers in other asthma phenotypes and the elevated blood leukocytes and eosinophils in paucigranulocytic asthmatics establish that systemic inflammatory activation characterizes all asthma phenotypes relative to health.

## Clinical Characteristics of Paucigranulocytic Asthma: The Apparent Paradox

Paucigranulocytic asthma presents an apparent clinical paradox that has contributed to its historical characterization as "non-inflammatory." Compared to other asthma phenotypes, paucigranulocytic asthmatics demonstrate favorable clinical metrics in most cases. **Median forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV₁) percentage of predicted values was 80.5% in paucigranulocytic asthma compared to 68-71.5% in other phenotypes (p=0.009)** [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28407269/), indicating relatively preserved lung function. Additionally, **the rate of severe refractory asthma was significantly lower in paucigranulocytic asthma at 21.7%, compared to 41.6-43.7% in eosinophilic and mixed phenotypes (p=0.01)** [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28407269/).

However, this apparently benign clinical profile does not reflect true absence of inflammation. Rather, paucigranulocytic asthma represents a heterogeneous group that includes both genuinely mild cases with excellent symptom control and a subset of patients with unexpectedly poor outcomes despite low inflammatory markers. Importantly, **14.8% of paucigranulocytic patients have poor asthma control despite their low inflammatory phenotype** [[2]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28407269/). Furthermore, **approximately 10-15% of paucigranulocytic asthmatics (representing 5-10% of all treated asthma patients) exhibit poor disease control and increased exacerbation risk** [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf), demonstrating that the phenotype encompasses clinically distinct subpopulations.

This clinical heterogeneity within the paucigranulocytic group indicates that asthmatics with this inflammatory pattern show variable clinical courses. Some experience excellent symptom control consistent with genuinely mild disease, while others manifest inadequately controlled asthma despite the absence of prominent granulocytic infiltration. This pattern suggests that the paucigranulocytic phenotype encompasses multiple underlying pathobiological mechanisms, not all of which are captured by traditional inflammatory biomarkers.

## Mechanistic Understanding: Low-Grade Inflammation Independent of Granulocytes

Recent comprehensive review of the paucigranulocytic asthma literature provides crucial mechanistic insight into how inflammation persists despite low granulocytic counts. A 2022 evidence-based review explicitly characterizes paucigranulocytic asthma as representing a **"low-grade inflammatory disease," not a non-inflammatory condition** [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf). The review further states that the **"underlying inflammatory process seems to be of greater intensity compared to healthy controls,"** providing explicit endorsement of the inflammatory nature of this phenotype [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf).

The mechanistic basis for low-grade inflammation in paucigranulocytic asthma has been progressively elucidated and involves multiple pathophysiological pathways operating independent of classical granulocytic infiltration [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf):

### Structural Cell-Mediated Inflammation

The pathophysiology of paucigranulocytic asthma is characterized by **structural cell abnormalities (epithelial and smooth muscle cells) that mediate inflammation independent of high granulocytic infiltration** [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf). Rather than relying on recruited inflammatory cells, the airway structural cells themselves participate directly in inflammatory processes. **Mast cell infiltration of airway smooth muscle** represents a critical mechanism, with **airway smooth muscle hyperplasia and hypertrophy** providing a structural basis for airway dysfunction [[6]](https://www.remedypublications.com/open-access/clinical-features-and-management-of-paucigranulocytic-asthma-6259.pdf) [[7]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2020.00191/full).

### Neurogenic Mechanisms

**Neurogenic factors including nerve growth factor (NGF) and parasympathetic dysregulation** contribute to inflammatory activation independent of granulocytic recruitment [[6]](https://www.remedypublications.com/open-access/clinical-features-and-management-of-paucigranulocytic-asthma-6259.pdf). These neural mechanisms activate intrinsic airway defenses and mediate local inflammatory responses through direct neural signaling.

### Mast Cell-Derived Mediators

**Activated mast cells release multiple inflammatory mediators including histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and prostaglandin D2 (PGD2)** [[6]](https://www.remedypublications.com/open-access/clinical-features-and-management-of-paucigranulocytic-asthma-6259.pdf). These potent inflammatory molecules activate airway smooth muscle and epithelial cells, driving airway hyperresponsiveness independent of granulocytic infiltration. **Cytokine, chemokine, and growth factor release from airway smooth muscle and mast cells** perpetuates the inflammatory environment [[6]](https://www.remedypublications.com/open-access/clinical-features-and-management-of-paucigranulocytic-asthma-6259.pdf).

### Airway Remodeling and Fixed Obstruction

**Airway remodeling and fixed airway obstruction occur via structural mechanisms independent of traditional inflammatory infiltration** [[6]](https://www.remedypublications.com/open-access/clinical-features-and-management-of-paucigranulocytic-asthma-6259.pdf) [[7]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2020.00191/full). Collagen deposition, smooth muscle proliferation, and epithelial dysfunction create persistent alterations in airway structure that maintain both airway dysfunction and inflammatory signaling even in the absence of active granulocyte recruitment. Notably, **approximately 25-30% of severe asthmatics previously classified as "non-inflammatory" are found to have the paucigranulocytic phenotype WITH concurrent airway remodeling** [[7]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2020.00191/full), indicating that structural inflammation occurs alongside cellular patterns that would traditionally be termed "non-inflammatory."

### Gene Expression Patterns

Gene expression studies of paucigranulocytic asthma tissue reveal a distinctive pattern—**"decreased immune cell infiltration and function" without absence of inflammation** [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf). This finding indicates that the inflammatory milieu persists at the molecular level despite reduced recruitment of classical inflammatory cells, supporting the concept of alternative inflammatory pathways sustaining the disease state.

## Inflammatory Biomarker Profile in Paucigranulocytic Asthma

The biomarker profile of paucigranulocytic asthma reflects its distinctive inflammatory pattern. **Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), a marker of eosinophilic airway inflammation, remains low (<30 ppb) in the paucigranulocytic phenotype** [[6]](https://www.remedypublications.com/open-access/clinical-features-and-management-of-paucigranulocytic-asthma-6259.pdf), which appears counterintuitive given the presence of elevated sputum and blood eosinophils. This apparent discordance highlights the complexity of inflammatory phenotyping and suggests that FeNO may not fully capture eosinophilic activation in non-classical disease patterns.

When compared to other asthma phenotypes, **interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and interleukin-8 (IL-8) levels in paucigranulocytic asthma are lower than in neutrophilic asthma but remain present** [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf). Similarly, **eosinophilic cationic protein (ECP), a marker of eosinophil activation, is lower in paucigranulocytic asthma compared to eosinophilic asthma but still measurable** [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf), again indicating reduced but present inflammatory marker elevation. **Levels of matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) and neutrophil elastase are lower than in other phenotypes but not normalized to healthy control levels** [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf), suggesting persistent protease activity and tissue remodeling.

This biomarker profile—characterized by relative reduction rather than absence of inflammatory markers—is consistent with the concept of low-grade inflammation. The markers remain elevated relative to health while showing lower absolute levels than phenotypes with higher granulocytic infiltration.

## Treatment Implications and Phenotype Validation

The clinical treatment response of paucigranulocytic asthmatics provides additional evidence supporting the inflammatory nature of this phenotype, albeit with distinctive mechanistic characteristics. **Paucigranulocytic asthmatics are unresponsive to corticosteroids and anti-interleukin-5 (anti-IL-5) biologic therapies** [[6]](https://www.remedypublications.com/open-access/clinical-features-and-management-of-paucigranulocytic-asthma-6259.pdf), which proves ineffective because these treatments target eosinophilic and classical inflammatory pathways not dominant in this phenotype.

Instead, **paucigranulocytic asthmatics require alternative therapies including long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMA), phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitors, c-kit receptor inhibitors, and bronchial thermoplasty** [[6]](https://www.remedypublications.com/open-access/clinical-features-and-management-of-paucigranulocytic-asthma-6259.pdf). These alternative approaches target distinct pathways—neural dysfunction, mast cell function, and structural remodeling—demonstrating that the inflammatory basis of paucigranulocytic asthma differs mechanistically from other phenotypes. The requirement for alternative therapies validates that inflammation persists but operates through non-classical mechanisms.

A critical complication in phenotype management is **the lack of traditional diagnostic biomarkers in paucigranulocytic asthma, including absent elevation of FeNO, periostin, and dipeptidyl peptidase-4** [[6]](https://www.remedypublications.com/open-access/clinical-features-and-management-of-paucigranulocytic-asthma-6259.pdf), which complicates treatment targeting and phenotype validation. However, some patient subsets show responsiveness to corticosteroids, suggesting that **certain paucigranulocytic clusters incorporate low-grade eosinophilic components** [[9]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2022.969243/full), indicating further heterogeneity within this phenotypic category.

## Terminology Precision: "Non-Inflammatory" Versus "Low-Grade Inflammatory"

A critical distinction exists between the designation of paucigranulocytic asthma based on sputum granulocyte patterns and the inflammatory status of the disease. Some educational materials describe paucigranulocytic asthma as representing "non-inflammatory asthma" [[5]](https://asthma.net/living/subgroups-the-4-types-of-airway-inflammation), but this terminology directly contradicts evidence-based findings. The term "paucigranulocytic" refers specifically to the sputum granulocyte infiltration pattern (few granulocytes), not to the overall inflammatory status of the disease.

More accurate terminology characterizes paucigranulocytic asthma as a **"low-grade inflammatory" or "reduced granulocytic inflammatory" phenotype** [[4]](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/223f/98ec57bba7936f13916d6b13f74b862630b6.pdf), acknowledging both the reduced granulocytic infiltration relative to other asthma subtypes and the persistent inflammatory processes demonstrated through elevated systemic markers and mechanistic studies. This terminology correctly reflects the dual reality: reduced classical granulocytic infiltration coupled with measurable airway and systemic inflammation through alternative pathways.

## Synthesis: Answering the Central Question

The evidence comprehensively addresses the core question: Are paucigranulocytic asthmatics really non-inflammatory? The answer is definitively **no**. Multiple lines of evidence converge on this conclusion:

**Sputum-based evidence** demonstrates that paucigranulocytic asthmatics exhibit elevated eosinophils compared to healthy controls despite their classification as "paucigranulocytic." This finding directly challenges the notion that paucigranulocytic asthma lacks inflammatory markers—rather, it demonstrates that these patients have eosinophilic inflammation even though their overall sputum granulocyte count is low.

**Systemic inflammatory markers** in paucigranulocytic asthmatics show elevated blood leukocytes and increased absolute blood eosinophils compared to healthy subjects, indicating systemic inflammatory activation despite limited airway granulocytic infiltration. This compartmentalization pattern—high systemic eosinophils with low airway granulocytes—characterizes the phenotype and demonstrates persistent systemic inflammation.

**Mechanistic understanding** reveals that paucigranulocytic asthma operates through alternative inflammatory pathways centered on mast cell activation, structural cell-mediated inflammation, and neurogenic mechanisms. These mechanisms sustain inflammatory signaling and airway dysfunction independent of classical granulocytic infiltration. The presence of airway remodeling in a substantial subset of paucigranulocytic asthmatics indicates that structural inflammation and fibrotic processes contribute to the disease phenotype.

**Clinical heterogeneity** within the paucigranulocytic group, with 10-15% of patients manifesting poor asthma control and increased exacerbation risk despite low inflammatory markers, demonstrates that this phenotype encompasses both genuinely mild disease and inflammatory asthma driven by non-classical mechanisms.

**Treatment responsiveness** patterns validate the inflammatory basis of paucigranulocytic asthma. The requirement for alternative therapies targeting mast cell function, neural pathways, and structural remodeling proves that inflammation persists but requires mechanisms-specific therapeutic approaches rather than the anti-eosinophilic and corticosteroid strategies effective for other phenotypes.

## Conclusions and Clinical Implications

Paucigranulocytic asthma represents a distinctive inflammatory phenotype characterized by low-grade but persistent airway and systemic inflammation independent of classical granulocytic infiltration. The evidence from a large cross-sectional study of 833 asthmatics provides definitive demonstration that paucigranulocytic asthmatics are not truly non-inflammatory—they exhibit elevated sputum and blood eosinophils, increased systemic leukocytes, and activated alternative inflammatory pathways relative to healthy controls.

The term "paucigranulocytic" appropriately describes the sputum cell count pattern but should not be misinterpreted as indicating absence of inflammation. Mechanistically, this phenotype operates through mast cell-mediated, neurogenic, and structural pathways that maintain inflammatory activity and airway dysfunction despite reduced granulocytic recruitment. Clinically, paucigranulocytic asthma encompasses heterogeneous disease severity, with most patients experiencing mild to moderate symptoms but a meaningful subset showing poor control and exacerbation risk.

Understanding paucigranulocytic asthma as a low-grade inflammatory condition rather than a non-inflammatory disease has important implications for both research and clinical practice. It justifies continued anti-inflammatory therapeutic approaches while recognizing that standard corticosteroid and anti-IL-5 therapies prove inadequate, necessitating alternative mechanisms-based treatments targeting mast cell activation, neurogenic factors, and airway remodeling. Furthermore, it emphasizes the importance of comprehensive inflammatory assessment in asthma management, recognizing that traditional biomarkers may not fully capture the inflammatory burden in this phenotype, and that multimodal approaches incorporating systemic markers, sputum analysis, and clinical assessment provide more complete disease characterization than any single inflammatory measure.

question: Is Panton-Valentine leucocidin associated with the pathogenesis of Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia in the UK?
context:
The morbidity and mortality associated with Panton-Valentine leucocidin (PVL)-positive Staphylococcus aureus suggest that this toxin is a key marker of disease severity. Nevertheless, the importance of PVL in the pathogenesis of primary bacteraemia caused by S. aureus is uncertain. We have determined the prevalence of PVL-encoding genes among isolates of S. aureus from bacteraemic patients.

Consecutive bacteraemia isolates of S. aureus (n=244) from patients hospitalized in 25 centres in the UK and Ireland during 2005 were screened for PVL and mecA genes. PVL-positive isolates were characterized by toxin gene profiling, PFGE, spa-typing and MIC determinations for a range of antimicrobials.

Four out of 244 isolates (1.6%) were PVL-positive and susceptible to oxacillin [methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA)]. Eighty-eight out of 244 (36%) were oxacillin-resistant (methicillin-resistant S. aureus), but none was PVL-positive. The four patients (two males: 30 and 33 years; two females: 62 and 80 years) had infection foci of: skin and soft tissue, unknown, indwelling line, and surgical site, and were located at one centre in Wales, one in England and two in Ireland. One of four PVL-positive isolates was resistant to penicillin and fusidic acid, the remainder were susceptible to all antibiotics tested. Genotypic analyses showed that the four isolates represented three distinct strains; the two isolates from Ireland were related.
long_answer: We found that 1.6% of S. aureus (all MSSA) from bacteraemic patients were PVL-positive. This low incidence suggests that PVL-positive S. aureus are of no particular significance as causative agents of S. aureus bacteraemia.
